SLIDE 6 — BODY, BRAIN, AND AGENT
Suggested duration: 90–120 seconds

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
Think of the interface as the body, and the AI model as the brain.
The interface is where we type and read. The model processes the request.
One interface can connect to different models. We can choose a model for the task instead of rebuilding the whole app.
The model names on this diagram are illustrative, not a list of verified products.
Now, add an agent: an application that connects a model to tools and context.
With permission, those tools can work with files, a browser, or an API.
The model chooses a step, the tool performs it, and the result comes back for checking.
The key difference is not just a smarter answer. It is a workflow that can take action.
Let’s compare this with tasks from school life.

Follow the visual stages: interface and model, multiple models, then agent on laptop. Pause for the model-cluster transfer. ‘Body’ and ‘brain’ are analogies. Tool access depends on configuration and authorization; an agent does not automatically control every app.

Ý CHÍNH TIẾNG VIỆT
Giao diện là thân, model là não theo phép ví von. Agent nối model với công cụ và ngữ cảnh để thực hiện rồi kiểm tra từng bước.

SLIDE 7 — THREE CHALLENGES
Suggested duration: 2–3 minutes

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
Let’s compare three ways to work: asking ChatGPT, using an AI-equipped laptop, and doing the task manually.
First: ‘Tell me about CIA Academy in the Philippines.’
This is public information. Search and AI can both help, but facts still need verification.
Second: ‘Get my current CIA schedule.’
That information is private. An unconnected chat cannot read it. A person or an agent needs authorized access to the school system.
Third: rearrange a schedule with several conditions.
We need to keep the class count and types, avoid overlaps, consider preferred teachers, and check next week and class sizes.
In this example, Self Writing must come before Writing in the afternoon.
The task is not finished when we find one empty cell. We must check the whole proposed timetable.
These are illustrative demonstrations, not live registrations.
The next slide shows how the workflow works.

DELIVERY CUES

Ý CHÍNH TIẾNG VIỆT
Ba mức: thông tin công khai, dữ liệu riêng cần quyền truy cập, và xếp lịch nhiều ràng buộc. Phải kiểm toàn lịch và sĩ số, không chỉ tìm ô trống.

SLIDE 8 — HOW THE WORKFLOW WORKS
Suggested duration: 75–100 seconds

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
On the left is a typical chat workflow.
The question goes from our device to a remote model. When search is available, the model can use it and summarize the results.
On the right is an agent workflow.
We give it a task and context. The model selects a tool, the tool runs, and the agent checks the result.
If the result is not enough, the process repeats.
The CIA example illustrates opening an authorized system, reading the timetable, and checking the requested conditions.
The model may still run in the cloud; the tools can run on a connected computer.
This does not mean every chat lacks tools, or that every agent has unlimited access.
The useful distinction is what tools and permissions are connected—and whether the result has been verified.
Now, let’s move from an engineering workflow to a learning problem.

DELIVERY CUES
Trace one path at a time, then show the CIA loop/demo control available on the slide. Keep cloud model and local tool execution distinct. The animation is a simulation, not evidence of completed live work.

Ý CHÍNH TIẾNG VIỆT
Chat và agent đều có thể dùng model từ xa. Agent có vòng giao nhiệm vụ, gọi công cụ, nhận kết quả, kiểm tra và lặp; quyền truy cập quyết định phạm vi làm được.

SLIDE 9 — TEN UNFAMILIAR WORDS
Suggested duration: 90–120 seconds, plus animation

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
Imagine you open your vocabulary book and meet ten unfamiliar words.
What do you do?
You look up the meanings, find the pronunciations, translate the examples, and write the words down.
Then you write them again—and again.
That takes time. But does copying mean we can remember and use them?
Let’s try the next-morning test.
Sometimes a word looks familiar on the page, but we cannot recall it when we need it.
That was the problem I wanted to solve: make the steps easier to manage, then bring the words back for review.
Instead of only asking AI for another explanation, I asked: could I build a tool for my own learning?

DELIVERY CUES
Ask the audience before narrating the lookup stages. Allow the sequence to reach ‘Remember them now?’, then click ‘Next morning’. Wait for the recall result. The book layout is recreated from a reference; the test is illustrative. Do not claim copying never helps or that the app guarantees memory.

Ý CHÍNH TIẾNG VIỆT
Tra nghĩa, phát âm, dịch ví dụ và chép mất nhiều bước; quen mặt chữ chưa chắc gọi lại được. Dẫn sang ý tưởng công cụ hỗ trợ học và ôn.

SLIDE 10 — VIBE CODING
Suggested duration: 60–90 seconds, plus video

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
If AI writes the code, what do we do?
Watch this short clip. Who is the programmer here?
The clip is a joke, but it introduces an idea called vibe coding.
We describe what we want, AI creates a working draft, and we try it.
Then we give specific feedback: ‘Add a Listen button.’ ‘Make the text bigger.’ ‘Fix this error.’
The human still decides what to build and checks whether it works.
Security, privacy, and data handling still matter.
This is how I approached my English-learning app: start from a real problem, build a small version, and improve it through testing.
Here is the result.

DELIVERY CUES
Play the video manually; do not speak over its main moment. Ask the question, then click ‘Decode the video’. Explain the three steps. The clip is a meme, not proof of a real development workflow.

Ý CHÍNH TIẾNG VIỆT
Mô tả nhu cầu, AI tạo bản thử, con người dùng thử và sửa. AI viết code không loại bỏ trách nhiệm kiểm tra bảo mật, dữ liệu và kết quả.

SLIDE 11 — ENGLISH — EVERYDAY LEARNING
Suggested duration: 75–100 seconds

SCRIPT (ENGLISH)
This is my English-learning app.
The goal is to bring the steps we saw in the book into one learning space.
I can look up words and save them in My Words, so I can come back to review.
For listening practice, I can start from an image or an audio file.
For writing, AI can suggest a more natural sentence and explain the change.
For grammar, it can break a sentence into parts such as subject, verb, and object.
And when I have a follow-up question, I can ask while I am learning.
The slide combines real screenshots with illustrative feature animations. It is not a live demonstration of every feature.
The app does not replace teachers or regular practice. It helps me organize the work and return to it.
My main message is this: start with a problem you understand, use AI to build something useful, and keep checking and improving it.
Thank you. What would you like to build?
